{{Short description|Branch of algebraic topology}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Topological ''K''-theory}}
In [[mathematics]], '''topological {{mvar|K}}-theory''' is a branch of [[algebraic topology]]. It was founded to study [[vector bundle]]s on [[topological space]]s, by means of ideas now recognised as (general) [[K-theory]] that were introduced by [[Alexander Grothendieck]]. The early work on topological {{mvar|K}}-theory is due to [[Michael Atiyah]] and [[Friedrich Hirzebruch]].

== Definitions ==
Let {{mvar|X}} be a [[compact space|compact]] [[Hausdorff space]] and <math>k= \R</math> or <math>\Complex</math>. Then <math>K_k(X)</math> is defined to be the [[Grothendieck group]] of the [[commutative monoid]] of [[isomorphism class]]es of finite-dimensional {{mvar|k}}-vector bundles over {{mvar|X}} under [[Whitney sum]]. [[Whitney sum#Operations on vector bundles|Tensor product]] of bundles gives {{mvar|K}}-theory a [[commutative ring]] structure. Without subscripts, <math>K(X)</math> usually denotes complex {{mvar|K}}-theory whereas real {{mvar|K}}-theory is sometimes written as <math>KO(X)</math>. The remaining discussion is focused on complex {{mvar|K}}-theory.

As a first example, note that the {{mvar|K}}-theory of a point is the integers. This is because vector bundles over a point are trivial and thus classified by their rank and the Grothendieck group of the natural numbers is the integers.

There is also a reduced version of {{mvar|K}}-theory, <math>\widetilde{K}(X)</math>, defined for {{mvar|X}} a compact [[pointed space]] (cf. [[reduced homology]]). This reduced theory is intuitively {{math|''K''(''X'')}} modulo [[trivial bundle]]s. It is defined as the group of stable equivalence classes of bundles. Two bundles {{mvar|E}} and {{mvar|F}} are said to be '''stably isomorphic''' if there are trivial bundles <math>\varepsilon_1</math> and <math>\varepsilon_2</math>, so that <math>E \oplus \varepsilon_1 \cong F\oplus  \varepsilon_2</math>. This equivalence relation results in a group since every vector bundle can be completed to a trivial bundle by summing with its orthogonal complement. Alternatively, <math>\widetilde{K}(X)</math> can be defined as the [[kernel of a homomorphism|kernel]] of the map <math>K(X)\to K(x_0) \cong \Z</math> induced by the inclusion of the base point {{math|''x''<sub>0</sub>}} into {{mvar|X}}.

{{mvar|K}}-theory forms a multiplicative (generalized) [[Cohomology#Cohomology theories|cohomology theory]] as follows. The [[short exact sequence]] of a pair of pointed spaces {{math|(''X'', ''A'')}}

:<math>\widetilde{K}(X/A) \to \widetilde{K}(X) \to \widetilde{K}(A)</math>

extends to a [[long exact sequence]]

:<math>\cdots \to \widetilde{K}(SX) \to \widetilde{K}(SA) \to \widetilde{K}(X/A) \to \widetilde{K}(X) \to \widetilde{K}(A).</math>

Let {{math|''S<sup>n</sup>''}} be the {{mvar|n}}-th [[Suspension (topology)|reduced suspension]] of a space and then define

:<math>\widetilde{K}^{-n}(X):=\widetilde{K}(S^nX), \qquad n\geq 0.</math>

Negative indices are chosen so that the [[coboundary]] maps increase dimension.

It is often useful to have an unreduced version of these groups, simply by defining:

:<math>K^{-n}(X)=\widetilde{K}^{-n}(X_+).</math>

Here <math>X_+</math> is <math>X</math> with a disjoint basepoint labeled '+' adjoined.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hatcher|title=Vector Bundles and K-theory|pages=57|url=https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf|accessdate=27 July 2017}}</ref>

Finally, the [[Bott periodicity theorem]] as formulated below extends the theories to positive integers.

== Properties ==
* <math>K^n</math> (respectively, <math>\widetilde{K}^n</math>) is a [[contravariant functor]] from the [[homotopy category]] of (pointed) spaces to the category of commutative rings. Thus, for instance, the {{mvar|K}}-theory over [[contractible space]]s is always <math>\Z.</math>
* The [[Spectrum (homotopy theory)|spectrum]] of {{mvar|K}}-theory is <math>BU\times\Z</math> (with the discrete topology on <math>\Z</math>), i.e. <math>K(X) \cong [ X_+, \Z \times BU ],</math> where {{math|[ , ]}} denotes pointed homotopy classes and {{math|''BU''}} is the [[colimit]] of the classifying spaces of the [[unitary group]]s: <math>BU(n) \cong \operatorname{Gr} (n, \Complex^{\infty} ).</math> Similarly, <math display="block">\widetilde{K}(X) \cong [X, \Z \times BU].</math> For real {{mvar|K}}-theory use {{math|''BO''}}.
* There is a [[natural homomorphism|natural]] [[ring homomorphism]] <math>K^0(X) \to H^{2*}(X, \Q),</math> the [[Chern character]], such that <math>K^0(X) \otimes \Q \to H^{2*}(X, \Q)</math> is an isomorphism.
* The equivalent of the [[Steenrod operation]]s in {{mvar|K}}-theory are the [[Adams operation]]s. They can be used to define characteristic classes in topological {{mvar|K}}-theory.
* The [[Splitting principle]] of topological {{mvar|K}}-theory allows one to reduce statements about arbitrary vector bundles to statements about sums of line bundles.
* The [[Thom isomorphism theorem]] in topological {{mvar|K}}-theory is <math display="block">K(X)\cong\widetilde{K}(T(E)),</math> where {{math|''T''(''E'')}} is the [[Thom space]] of the vector bundle {{mvar|E}} over {{mvar|X}}. This holds whenever {{mvar|E}} is a spin-bundle.
* The [[Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence]] allows computation of {{mvar|K}}-groups from ordinary cohomology groups.
* Topological {{mvar|K}}-theory can be generalized vastly to a functor on [[C*-algebras]], see [[operator K-theory]] and [[KK-theory]].

== Bott periodicity ==
The phenomenon of [[Frequency|periodicity]] named after [[Raoul Bott]] (see [[Bott periodicity theorem]]) can be formulated this way:

* <math>K(X \times \mathbb{S}^2) = K(X) \otimes K(\mathbb{S}^2),</math> and <math>K(\mathbb{S}^2) = \Z[H]/(H-1)^2</math> where ''H'' is the class of the [[tautological bundle]] on <math>\mathbb{S}^2 = \mathbb{P}^1(\Complex),</math> i.e. the [[Riemann sphere]].
* <math>\widetilde{K}^{n+2}(X)=\widetilde{K}^n(X).</math>
* <math>\Omega^2 BU \cong BU \times \Z.</math>

In real {{mvar|K}}-theory there is a similar periodicity, but modulo 8.

== Applications ==
Topological {{mvar|K}}-theory has been applied in [[Frank Adams|John Frank Adams’]] proof of the “[[Hopf invariant]] one” problem via [[Adams operation]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Adams |first=John |title=On the non-existence of elements of Hopf invariant one |date=1960 |publisher=Ann. Math. 72 1}}</ref> Adams also proved an upper bound for the number of linearly-independent [[vector fields on spheres]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Adams |first=John |date=1962 |title=Vector Fields on Spheres |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=75 |issue=3 |pages=603–632 |doi=10.2307/1970213 |jstor=1970213 }}</ref>

== Chern character ==
[[Michael Atiyah]] and [[Friedrich Hirzebruch]] proved a theorem relating the topological K-theory of a finite CW complex <math>X</math> with its rational cohomology. In particular, they showed that there exists a homomorphism

:<math>ch : K^*_{\text{top}}(X)\otimes\Q \to H^*(X;\Q)</math>

such that

:<math>\begin{align}
K^0_{\text{top}}(X)\otimes \Q & \cong \bigoplus_k H^{2k}(X;\Q) \\
K^1_{\text{top}}(X)\otimes \Q & \cong \bigoplus_k H^{2k+1}(X;\Q) 
\end{align}</math>

There is an algebraic analogue relating the Grothendieck group of coherent sheaves and the Chow ring of a smooth projective variety <math>X</math>.
